reviewScope.rolePreserved: Design and review failure tests and controlled experiments, with observed outcomes and explicit coverage limits; no delivery-policy implementation mandate.
successCriteria: Crash recovery tests reach an actual commit/acknowledgement boundary in the effective consumer wiring.
The claimed redelivery is broker-driven and correlated to the interrupted logical message.
Protected effects, protocol completion, observation bounds and cleanup are checked separately.
Missing injection coverage cannot be reported as a system guarantee or system defect.
Different acknowledgement modes change the feasible test rather than being silently replaced in test configuration.
reviewScope.compatibility: Existing target inspection remains: Java 21 is needed only for the existing virtual-thread fragment; lower targets retain existing executors. No new executable Java, dependency or runtime upgrade added.

findingsCorrected.priorGap: The previous kill-between-commit-and-ack instruction specified the desired instant but did not establish that effective acknowledgement wiring left it open or that the kill landed there.
findingsCorrected.consequence: A post-ack restart can leave one business row and pass the final-state test without exercising redelivery or deduplication.
findingsCorrected.correction: Require actual subscription/transaction/ack wiring, a controlled hold after authoritative commit and before any acknowledgement, confirmed process exit, and broker redelivery plus protected outcome.
findingsCorrected.evidence: RabbitMQ 4.3 AMQP 0-9-1 acknowledgement documentation and the Java client registration API; derived controlled-fixture reasoning.

findingsCorrected.priorGap: The short crash recipe did not distinguish coverage failure from a violated recovery contract, or prevent manual replay from substituting for broker recovery.
findingsCorrected.consequence: Tests can overclaim resilience from an unexercised failure or misdiagnose missing fixture coverage.
findingsCorrected.correction: Add bounded controller ordering, independent cleanup, no-crash and post-ack coverage controls, and separate missing-boundary/inconclusive outcomes from reached-boundary violations.
findingsCorrected.evidence: Logical oracle analysis grounded in the actual acknowledgement contract; not a measured agent improvement.

# Crash-recovery review fixture

This is a review fixture with source excerpts, not a buildable application.
Runtime: Java 17, RabbitMQ 4.3 speaking AMQP 0-9-1, RabbitMQ Java client API, PostgreSQL 16.
The accepted service contract is at-least-once processing after consumer failure with one committed ledger effect per message ID.
The production and integration-test launcher both load runtime.env unchanged.
Only the consumer process is killed. The broker and authoritative PostgreSQL primary remain alive; no other fault is injected.
There is one consumer, one channel and one uniquely identified message in each isolated case. No framework adds acknowledgement callbacks.
Ledger.applyOnceAndCommit uses a real transaction with a unique message ID and a ledger write in the same transaction; it returns only after commit.
The test controller queries that primary using a separate connection and can inspect broker deliveries, consumer registrations and acknowledgement/unacknowledged state.
The existing test-only Hooks implementation can arm a message ID, signal when afterCommit is reached and keep that callback blocked until released or the consumer dies. It times out after 40 seconds. Production hooks are no-ops.
The controller can wait for that signal for 5 seconds, force-kill the exact consumer process, verify its exit within 5 seconds, and start a fresh process with hooks disarmed. It can wait at most 30 seconds for recovery and has a separate 10-second cleanup watchdog.
The controller records message IDs and delivery attempts independently from ledger effects. A successful publisher confirm establishes that the single message was accepted by the isolated queue.

# Existing crash test

Claim: the green run proves consumer crash recovery and duplicate suppression.

1. Launch the isolated broker, database and consumer using runtime.env.
2. Publish message m-42 with publisher confirmation.
3. Sleep 100 milliseconds.
4. Force-kill the consumer and wait for exit, at most 5 seconds.
5. Restart it and wait up to 30 seconds for the health endpoint.
6. Assert that the ledger contains exactly one row for m-42.

Fixture cleanup has an independent 10-second watchdog.
